claim: Positive-sense RNA viruses hijack intracellular membranes that provide niches for viral RNA synthesis and a platform for interactions with host proteins.
source: Positive-sense RNA viruses hijack intracellular membranes that provide niches for viral RNA synthesis and a platform for interactions with host proteins.
evidence: This is a general statement about positive-sense RNA viruses supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: A biotin ligase was engineered into a coronaviral replication/transcription complex (RTC).
source: We engineered a biotin ligase into a coronaviral replication/transcription complex (RTC) and identified >500 host proteins constituting the RTC microenvironment.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach of engineering BirAR118G into the MHV RTC.

claim: More than 500 host proteins constitute the RTC microenvironment.
source: We engineered a biotin ligase into a coronaviral replication/transcription complex (RTC) and identified >500 host proteins constituting the RTC microenvironment.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript showing 513 significantly enriched host proteins.

claim: siRNA-silencing demonstrated importance of vesicular trafficking pathways for coronavirus replication.
source: siRNA-silencing of each RTC-proximal host factor demonstrated importance of vesicular trafficking pathways, ubiquitin-dependent and autophagy-related processes, and translation initiation factors.
evidence: The siRNA screen data presented in Figure 4 shows that silencing of factors in vesicular trafficking pathways reduced viral replication.

claim: siRNA-silencing demonstrated importance of ubiquitin-dependent processes for coronavirus replication.
source: siRNA-silencing of each RTC-proximal host factor demonstrated importance of vesicular trafficking pathways, ubiquitin-dependent and autophagy-related processes, and translation initiation factors.
evidence: The siRNA screen data shows that silencing of ubiquitin-dependent factors reduced viral replication.

claim: siRNA-silencing demonstrated importance of autophagy-related processes for coronavirus replication.
source: siRNA-silencing of each RTC-proximal host factor demonstrated importance of vesicular trafficking pathways, ubiquitin-dependent and autophagy-related processes, and translation initiation factors.
evidence: The siRNA screen data shows that silencing of autophagy-related factors reduced viral replication.

claim: siRNA-silencing demonstrated importance of translation initiation factors for coronavirus replication.
source: siRNA-silencing of each RTC-proximal host factor demonstrated importance of vesicular trafficking pathways, ubiquitin-dependent and autophagy-related processes, and translation initiation factors.
evidence: The siRNA screen data shows that silencing of translation initiation factors significantly reduced viral replication.

claim: Translation initiation factors were detected at the RTC.
source: Notably, detection of translation initiation factors at the RTC was instrumental to visualize and demonstrate active translation proximal to replication complexes of several coronaviruses.
evidence: Mass spectrometry data identified translation initiation factors as RTC-proximal, and immunofluorescence/proximity ligation assays confirmed their localization.

claim: Active translation occurs proximal to replication complexes of several coronaviruses.
source: Notably, detection of translation initiation factors at the RTC was instrumental to visualize and demonstrate active translation proximal to replication complexes of several coronaviruses.
evidence: Ribopuromycylation assays shown in Figures 6 and 7 demonstrate active translation near viral RTCs for MHV, HCoV-229E, and MERS-CoV.

claim: Coronaviruses induce membrane modifications that materialize as an ER-derived network of interconnected double-membrane vesicles (DMVs) and convoluted membranes (CM).
source: Ultrastructural studies have reported the origin, nature, and extent of membrane modifications induced by coronaviruses (order Nidovirales, family Coronaviridae), which materialize as an ER-derived network of interconnected double-membrane vesicles (DMVs) and convoluted membranes (CM) in perinuclear regions of infected cells to which the viral replication/transcription complex (RTC) is anchored (Knoops et al., 2008; Ulasli et al., 2010; Oudshoorn et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous ultrastructural studies and confirmed by the APEX2 electron microscopy data in this manuscript.

claim: The coronavirus RTC is anchored to DMVs and CM in perinuclear regions of infected cells.
source: Ultrastructural studies have reported the origin, nature, and extent of membrane modifications induced by coronaviruses (order Nidovirales, family Coronaviridae), which materialize as an ER-derived network of interconnected double-membrane vesicles (DMVs) and convoluted membranes (CM) in perinuclear regions of infected cells to which the viral replication/transcription complex (RTC) is anchored (Knoops et al., 2008; Ulasli et al., 2010; Oudshoorn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and the APEX2-nsp2 electron microscopy data showing DAB staining at DMVs and CM.

claim: The coronavirus RTC is generated by translation of genomic RNA into two large polyproteins.
source: The RTC is generated by translation of the genomic RNA into two large polyproteins that are extensively auto-proteolytically processed by viral proteases to give rise to 16 processing end-products, termed non-structural proteins (nsps) 1–16.
evidence: This is established knowledge about coronavirus replication supported by the literature.

claim: Coronavirus polyproteins are extensively auto-proteolytically processed by viral proteases to give rise to 16 non-structural proteins (nsps 1-16).
source: The RTC is generated by translation of the genomic RNA into two large polyproteins that are extensively auto-proteolytically processed by viral proteases to give rise to 16 processing end-products, termed non-structural proteins (nsps) 1–16.
evidence: This is established knowledge about coronavirus polyprotein processing.

claim: Nsp1 is rapidly cleaved from the polyproteins and not considered an integral component of the coronaviral RTC.
source: Nsp1 is rapidly cleaved from the polyproteins and not considered an integral component of the coronaviral RTC, but interferes with host cell translation by inducing degradation of cellular mRNAs (Huang et al., 2011; Züst et al., 2007; Lokugamage et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and confirmed by the mass spectrometry data showing nsp1 was not enriched in the RTC-proximal proteome.

claim: Nsp1 interferes with host cell translation by inducing degradation of cellular mRNAs.
source: Nsp1 is rapidly cleaved from the polyproteins and not considered an integral component of the coronaviral RTC, but interferes with host cell translation by inducing degradation of cellular mRNAs (Huang et al., 2011; Züst et al., 2007; Lokugamage et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Nsps 2-16 are thought to comprise the RTC.
source: Although it has not yet been formally demonstrated, the remaining nsps (nsp2-16) are thought to comprise the RTC and harbor multiple enzymes and functions, such as de-ubiquitination, proteases, helicase, polymerase, exo- and endonuclease, and N7- and 2'O-methyltransferases (Thiel et al., 2003; Snijder et al., 2003; Decroly et al., 2008; Barretto et al., 2005; Lindner et al., 2005; Athmer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and confirmed by the mass spectrometry data showing nsp2-10 and nsp12-16 were enriched in the RTC-proximal proteome.

claim: The coronavirus RTC harbors multiple enzymes and functions including de-ubiquitination, proteases, helicase, polymerase, exo- and endonuclease, and N7- and 2'O-methyltransferases.
source: Although it has not yet been formally demonstrated, the remaining nsps (nsp2-16) are thought to comprise the RTC and harbor multiple enzymes and functions, such as de-ubiquitination, proteases, helicase, polymerase, exo- and endonuclease, and N7- and 2'O-methyltransferases (Thiel et al., 2003; Snijder et al., 2003; Decroly et al., 2008; Barretto et al., 2005; Lindner et al., 2005; Athmer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references describing the functions of individual nsps.

claim: BirAR118G biotinylates proximal (<10 nm) proteins in live cells without disrupting intracellular membranes or protein complexes.
source: BirAR118G biotinylates proximal (<10 nm) proteins in live cells without disrupting intracellular membranes or protein complexes, and hence, does not rely on high-affinity protein-protein interactions but is also able to permanently tag transient interactions (Roux et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference describing the BirAR118G proximity labeling method.

claim: BirAR118G does not rely on high-affinity protein-protein interactions but is able to permanently tag transient interactions.
source: BirAR118G biotinylates proximal (<10 nm) proteins in live cells without disrupting intracellular membranes or protein complexes, and hence, does not rely on high-affinity protein-protein interactions but is also able to permanently tag transient interactions (Roux et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference describing the properties of BirAR118G.

claim: Covalent protein biotinylation allows stringent lysis and washing conditions during affinity purification.
source: Covalent protein biotinylation allows stringent lysis and washing conditions during affinity purification and subsequent mass spectrometric identification of captured factors.
evidence: This is a known property of biotin-based affinity purification methods.

claim: MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2 was generated by inserting myc-tagged BirAR118G as an in-frame fusion to nsp2.
source: To insert the promiscuous biotin ligase BirAR118G as an integral subunit of the MHV RTC, we used a vaccinia virus-based reverse genetic system (Coley et al., 2005; Eriksson et al., 2008) to generate a recombinant MHV harboring an in-frame fusion of myc-tagged BirAR118G to nsp2.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used to generate the recombinant virus.

claim: MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2 retained the cleavage site between nsp1 and BirAR118G.
source: MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2 retained the cleavage site between nsp1 and BirAR118G, while a deleted cleavage site between BirAR118G and nsp2 ensured the expression of a BirAR118G-nsp2 fusion protein (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is shown in the genome organization diagram in Figure 1a.

claim: A deleted cleavage site between BirAR118G and nsp2 ensured the expression of a BirAR118G-nsp2 fusion protein.
source: MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2 retained the cleavage site between nsp1 and BirAR118G, while a deleted cleavage site between BirAR118G and nsp2 ensured the expression of a BirAR118G-nsp2 fusion protein (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is shown in the genome organization diagram in Figure 1a and confirmed by Western blot in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The insertion site between nsp1 and nsp2 was chosen because it was previously shown to tolerate large insertions within the MHV replicase polyprotein.
source: This strategy was chosen because it was recently employed by Freeman et al. for a fusion of green fluorescent protein (GFP) with nsp2 and represents the only known site tolerating large insertions within the MHV replicase polyprotein (Freeman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference to Freeman et al., 2014.

claim: MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2 replicated to comparable peak titers as the parental wild-type MHV-A59.
source: MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2 replicated to comparable peak titers and replication kinetics as the parental wild-type MHV-A59 (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is shown in the viral replication kinetics data in Figure 1b.

claim: MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2 had comparable replication kinetics as the parental wild-type MHV-A59.
source: MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2 replicated to comparable peak titers and replication kinetics as the parental wild-type MHV-A59 (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is shown in the viral replication kinetics data in Figure 1b.

claim: MHV-GFP-nsp2 reached wild-type virus peak titers with slightly reduced viral titers at 9 h.p.i. compared to MHV-A59 and MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2.
source: MHV-GFP-nsp2, which was constructed in parallel and contained the coding sequence of EGFP (Freeman et al., 2014) instead of BirAR118G, was used as a control and also reached wild-type virus peak titers, with slightly reduced viral titers at 9 hr post- infection (h.p.i.) compared to MHV-A59 and MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2 (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is shown in the viral replication kinetics data in Figure 1b.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed that the BirAR118G-nsp2 fusion protein is specifically detected in MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected cells.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed that the BirAR118G-nsp2 fusion protein is specifically detected in MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected cells and that the BirAR118G biotin ligase remains fused to nsp2 during MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2 infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The BirAR118G biotin ligase remains fused to nsp2 during MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2 infection.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed that the BirAR118G-nsp2 fusion protein is specifically detected in MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected cells and that the BirAR118G biotin ligase remains fused to nsp2 during MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2 infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: BirAR118G-nsp2 remained strongly associated with the MHV RTC throughout the entire replication cycle.
source: BirAR118G-nsp2 remained strongly associated with the MHV RTC throughout the entire replication cycle, as indicated by the co-localization of BirAR118G-nsp2 with established markers of the MHV replicase, such as nsp2/3 and nsp8 (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence microscopy data in Figure 1c and supplementary figures.

claim: BirAR118G-nsp2 co-localizes with established markers of the MHV replicase such as nsp2/3 and nsp8.
source: BirAR118G-nsp2 remained strongly associated with the MHV RTC throughout the entire replication cycle, as indicated by the co-localization of BirAR118G-nsp2 with established markers of the MHV replicase, such as nsp2/3 and nsp8 (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence microscopy data showing co-localization.

claim: Nsp2 co-localizes with other nsps of the coronaviral RTC.
source: This observation corroborates previous studies demonstrating that nsp2, although not required for viral RNA synthesis, co-localizes with other nsps of the coronaviral RTC (Schiller et al., 1998; Hagemeijer et al., 2010; Graham et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references and confirmed by the co-localization data in this study.

claim: Nsp2 is not required for viral RNA synthesis.
source: This observation corroborates previous studies demonstrating that nsp2, although not required for viral RNA synthesis, co-localizes with other nsps of the coronaviral RTC (Schiller et al., 1998; Hagemeijer et al., 2010; Graham et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Biotinylated proteins were readily detected with fluorophore-coupled streptavidin near the MHV RTC throughout the entire replication cycle in MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected cells when culture medium was supplemented with biotin.
source: Importantly, by supplementing the culture medium with biotin, we could readily detect biotinylated proteins with fluorophore-coupled streptavidin that appeared close to the MHV RTC throughout the entire replication cycle in MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected cells, demonstrating efficient proximity-dependent biotinylation of RTC-proximal host factors (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence microscopy data in Figure 1c and supplementary figures.

claim: APEX2-catalyzed DAB polymer deposition was readily detectable at characteristic coronavirus replication compartments such as DMVs and CM.
source: As shown in Figure 1d, APEX2-catalized DAB polymer deposition was readily detectable at characteristic coronavirus replication compartments, such as DMVs and CM, categorically demonstrating that the nsp2 fusion proteins localize to known sites of coronavirus replication (Knoops et al., 2008; Ulasli et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown by electron microscopy data in Figure 1d.

claim: Nsp2 fusion proteins localize to known sites of coronavirus replication.
source: As shown in Figure 1d, APEX2-catalized DAB polymer deposition was readily detectable at characteristic coronavirus replication compartments, such as DMVs and CM, categorically demonstrating that the nsp2 fusion proteins localize to known sites of coronavirus replication (Knoops et al., 2008; Ulasli et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the APEX2 electron microscopy data in Figure 1d.

claim: A characteristic pattern of endogenously biotinylated proteins was observed under all conditions where no exogenous biotin was added to the culture medium.
source: A characteristic pattern of endogenously biotinylated proteins was observed under all conditions where no exogenous biotin was added to the culture medium (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 2b.

claim: The addition of biotin in the absence of the BirAR118G biotin ligase does not recognizably change the fraction of endogenously biotinylated proteins.
source: The same pattern was detectable in non-infected and wild-type MHV-A59-infected cells when the culture medium was supplemented with biotin, suggesting that the addition of biotin in the absence of the BirAR118G biotin ligase does not recognizably change the fraction of endogenously biotinylated proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data in Figure 2b showing similar patterns.

claim: A greatly increased fraction of biotinylated proteins was observed in lysates derived from MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected cells treated with biotin.
source: In contrast, we observed a greatly increased fraction of biotinylated proteins in lysates derived from MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected cells treated with biotin.
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 2b.

claim: Virus-mediated expression of the BirAR118G biotin ligase results in efficient biotinylation when biotin is added to the culture medium.
source: This result demonstrates that virus-mediated expression of the BirAR118G biotin ligase results in efficient biotinylation when biotin is added to the culture medium.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data showing increased biotinylation in MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected cells with biotin supplementation.

claim: The fraction of biotinylated proteins can be readily affinity purified, enriched, and recovered under stringent denaturing lysis and washing conditions using streptavidin-coupled magnetic beads.
source: Moreover, we could readily affinity purify, enrich, and recover the fraction of biotinylated proteins under stringent denaturing lysis and washing conditions by using streptavidin-coupled magnetic beads (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 2b.

claim: Overall, 1381 host proteins were identified by LC-MS/MS.
source: Overall, 1381 host proteins were identified, of which 513 were statistically significantly enriched in MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected samples over MHV-A59-infected samples.
evidence: This is from the mass spectrometry analysis results.

claim: 513 host proteins were statistically significantly enriched in MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected samples over MHV-A59-infected samples.
source: Overall, 1381 host proteins were identified, of which 513 were statistically significantly enriched in MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected samples over MHV-A59-infected samples.
evidence: This is from the mass spectrometry analysis results shown in Figure 2c and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The 513 significantly enriched host proteins represent a comprehensive repertoire of RTC-proximal factors throughout MHV infection.
source: These host proteins represent a comprehensive repertoire of RTC-proximal factors throughout MHV infection (Figure 2c, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is the interpretation of the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Viral replicase gene products nsp2-10 and nsp12-16, and the nucleocapsid protein were significantly enriched in fractions derived from MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected cells.
source: Importantly, besides the 513 host proteins that were enriched in MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected cells, we noted that viral replicase gene products nsp2-10 and nsp12-16, and the nucleocapsid protein were also significantly enriched in fractions derived from MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected cells, suggesting that they are all in close proximity to the BirAR118G-nsp2 fusion protein (Figure 2c, Figure 2d).
evidence: This is shown in the mass spectrometry data in Figure 2c and 2d.

claim: Nsp2-10, nsp12-16, and nucleocapsid protein are all in close proximity to the BirAR118G-nsp2 fusion protein.
source: Importantly, besides the 513 host proteins that were enriched in MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected cells, we noted that viral replicase gene products nsp2-10 and nsp12-16, and the nucleocapsid protein were also significantly enriched in fractions derived from MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2-infected cells, suggesting that they are all in close proximity to the BirAR118G-nsp2 fusion protein (Figure 2c, Figure 2d).
evidence: This is inferred from the mass spectrometry data showing significant enrichment of these viral proteins.

claim: The enrichment of nsp2-10, nsp12-16, and nucleocapsid protein is in agreement with studies demonstrating co-localization and interactions amongst individual nsps and association of the nucleocapsid protein with the coronavirus RTC.
source: This is in agreement with studies demonstrating co-localization and interactions amongst individual nsps, and with studies showing association of the nucleocapsid protein with the coronavirus RTC (Ulasli et al., 2010; Denison et al., 1999; Sims et al., 2000; van der Meer et al., 1999; Bost et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The labeling approach demonstrates specificity and effectiveness in live cells.
source: It also highlights the specificity and effectiveness of the labeling approach in live cells and is the first experimental evidence showing that collectively these viral nsps and the nucleocapsid (N) protein are subunits of the coronavirus RTC.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful identification of expected viral RTC components.

claim: This is the first experimental evidence showing that collectively nsp2-10, nsp12-16, and the nucleocapsid protein are subunits of the coronavirus RTC.
source: It also highlights the specificity and effectiveness of the labeling approach in live cells and is the first experimental evidence showing that collectively these viral nsps and the nucleocapsid (N) protein are subunits of the coronavirus RTC.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Nsp1 is likely not an integral component of the coronavirus RTC.
source: Furthermore, these results corroborate previous reports that nsp1 is likely not an integral component of the coronavirus RTC (Huang et al., 2011; Züst et al., 2007; Lokugamage et al., 2015; Denison et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by cited references and confirmed by the mass spectrometry data showing nsp1 was not enriched.

claim: Nsp11 is a short peptide of only 14 amino acids at the carboxyterminus of polyprotein 1a with a yet unassigned role or function in coronavirus replication.
source: Amongst the 'not detected' or 'not enriched' viral proteins are (i) nsp11, which is a short peptide of only 14 amino acids at the carboxyterminus of polyprotein 1a with a yet unassigned role or function in coronavirus replication
evidence: This is established knowledge about nsp11.

claim: Structural proteins spike (S), envelope (E), and membrane (M) mainly localize to sites of viral assembly before being incorporated into newly-formed viral particles.
source: (ii) the structural proteins spike (S) protein, envelope (E) protein, and membrane (M) protein, which mainly localize to sites of viral assembly before being incorporated into newly-formed viral particles
evidence: This is established knowledge about coronavirus structural proteins.

claim: Structural proteins S, E, M and all accessory proteins were not detected or not enriched in the RTC-proximal proteome.
source: Amongst the 'not detected' or 'not enriched' viral proteins are (i) nsp11, which is a short peptide of only 14 amino acids at the carboxyterminus of polyprotein 1a with a yet unassigned role or function in coronavirus replication, (ii) the structural proteins spike (S) protein, envelope (E) protein, and membrane (M) protein, which mainly localize to sites of viral assembly before being incorporated into newly-formed viral particles, and (iii) all accessory proteins (NS2a, HE, ORF4, ORF5a).
evidence: This is shown in the mass spectrometry data in Figure 2d.

claim: The proximity-dependent biotinylation approach demonstrates specific and exclusive labeling of MHV-RTC-associated proteins.
source: Altogether, these results validate the proximity-dependent biotinylation approach and demonstrate the specific and exclusive labeling of MHV-RTC-associated proteins (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is inferred from the selective enrichment of expected RTC components and exclusion of non-RTC proteins.

claim: The identified RTC-proximal host proteins likely include proteins that display a prolonged co-localization with the MHV RTC.
source: Therefore, the identified RTC-proximal host proteins, recorded over the entire duration of the MHV replication cycle, likely include proteins that display a prolonged co-localization with the MHV RTC, proteins that may locate only transiently in close proximity to the RTC, and proteins of which only a minor fraction of the cellular pool may associate with the RTC.
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of the BirAR118G labeling method.

claim: The identified RTC-proximal host proteins likely include proteins that may locate only transiently in close proximity to the RTC.
source: Therefore, the identified RTC-proximal host proteins, recorded over the entire duration of the MHV replication cycle, likely include proteins that display a prolonged co-localization with the MHV RTC, proteins that may locate only transiently in close proximity to the RTC, and proteins of which only a minor fraction of the cellular pool may associate with the RTC.
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of the BirAR118G labeling method.

claim: The identified RTC-proximal host proteins likely include proteins of which only a minor fraction of the cellular pool may associate with the RTC.
source: Therefore, the identified RTC-proximal host proteins, recorded over the entire duration of the MHV replication cycle, likely include proteins that display a prolonged co-localization with the MHV RTC, proteins that may locate only transiently in close proximity to the RTC, and proteins of which only a minor fraction of the cellular pool may associate with the RTC.
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of the BirAR118G labeling method.

claim: RTN4 displays pronounced co-localization with the MHV RTC.
source: Accordingly, we identified RTC-proximal host proteins displaying a pronounced co-localization with the MHV RTC, such as the ER protein reticulon 4 (RTN4; Figure 2e)
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence microscopy data in Figure 2e.

claim: eIF3E co-localization with the MHV RTC was not readily detectable by indirect immunofluorescence microscopy.
source: and host proteins where co-localization by indirect immunofluorescence microscopy was not readily detectable, such as the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3E (eIF3E; Figure 2e).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence microscopy data in Figure 2e.

claim: Proximity ligation assay demonstrated proximity of eIF3E and dsRNA in MHV-infected cells.
source: However, in the latter case, a more sensitive detection technique, such as a proximity ligation assay that relies on proximity-dependent antibody-coupled DNA probe amplification (Söderberg et al., 2006), demonstrated proximity of eIF3E and dsRNA in MHV-infected cells (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is shown by proximity ligation assay data in Figure 2f.

claim: 86 GO biological process terms were significantly enriched in the RTC-proximal host protein dataset.
source: 86 GO biological process (BP) terms were significantly enriched in the dataset (p-value < 0.05), of which 32 terms were highly significant (p-value < 0.005) (Figure 3a, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is from the GO enrichment analysis results.

claim: 32 GO biological process terms were highly significant (p-value < 0.005) in the RTC-proximal host protein dataset.
source: 86 GO biological process (BP) terms were significantly enriched in the dataset (p-value < 0.05), of which 32 terms were highly significant (p-value < 0.005) (Figure 3a, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is from the GO enrichment analysis results shown in Figure 3a.

claim: 25 of the 32 highly significant GO BP terms fell into five broad functional categories: cell adhesion, transport, cell organization, translation, and catabolic processes.
source: Additional analysis using AmiGO revealed that 25 of these 32 highly significant GO BP terms fell into five broad functional categories, namely cell adhesion, transport, cell organization, translation, and catabolic processes.
evidence: This is from the AmiGO analysis of GO terms.

claim: The category 'transport' included protein trafficking and vesicular-mediated transport pathways and comprised the majority of RTC-proximal factors.
source: The category 'transport' included protein trafficking and vesicular-mediated transport pathways and comprised the majority of RTC-proximal factors (Figure 3a, Figure 3b).
evidence: This is from the GO enrichment and STRING network analysis.

claim: Protein interaction network analysis revealed at least four distinct clusters of interacting factors within the 'transport' category.
source: Protein interaction network analysis, using STRING, revealed at least four distinct clusters of interacting factors within this category (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is shown in the STRING network analysis in Figure 3b.

claim: Cluster I (protein transport) comprised nuclear transport receptors at nuclear pore complexes such as importins and transportins.
source: Cluster I, protein transport, comprised nuclear transport receptors at nuclear pore complexes, such as importins and transportins.
evidence: This is from the STRING network analysis of the transport category.

claim: Cluster I contained Sec63, which is part of the Sec61 translocon and has been implicated in protein translocation across ER membranes.
source: Interestingly, this cluster also contained Sec63, which is part of the Sec61 translocon (Rapoport, 2007) and has been implicated in protein translocation across ER membranes.
evidence: This is from the STRING network analysis and supported by the cited reference.

claim: The list of RTC-proximal factors included signal recognition particles SRP54a and SRP68 proteins that promote the transfer of newly synthetized integral membrane proteins or secreted proteins across translocon complexes.
source: The list of RTC-proximal factors also included signal recognition particles SRP54a and SRP68 proteins (Supplementary file 2) that promote the transfer of newly synthetized integral membrane proteins or secreted proteins across translocon complexes.
evidence: This is from the mass spectrometry data and established knowledge about SRP function.

claim: The list of RTC-proximal factors contained Naca and BTF3, which prevent the translocation of non-secretory proteins toward the ER lumen.
source: Furthermore, the list contained Naca and BTF3, which prevent the translocation of non-secretory proteins toward the ER lumen (Wiedmann et al., 1994; Gamerdinger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is from the mass spectrometry data and supported by the cited references.

claim: Cluster II included vesicle components, tethers and SNARE proteins characteristic of the COPII-mediated ER-to-Golgi apparatus anterograde vesicular transport pathway.
source: Cluster II included vesicle components, tethers and SNARE (Soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive-factor Attachment protein Receptor) proteins characteristic of the COPII-mediated ER-to-Golgi apparatus anterograde vesicular transport pathway
evidence: This is from the STRING network analysis of the transport category.

claim: Cluster III contained components of the COPI-related retrograde Golgi-to-ER transport machinery.
source: whereas, cluster III contained components of the COPI-related retrograde Golgi-to-ER transport machinery.
evidence: This is from the STRING network analysis of the transport category.

claim: Cluster IV was comprised of proteins that mediate clathrin-coated vesicle (endosomal) transport between the plasma membrane and the trans-Golgi network (TGN).
source: Moreover, Cluster IV was comprised of proteins that mediate clathrin-coated vesicle (endosomal) transport between the plasma membrane and the trans-Golgi network (TGN), which is also closely associated with the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is from the STRING network analysis of the transport category.

claim: Cluster IV components can be regarded as regulating late-Golgi trafficking events and interacting with the endosomal system.
source: Together with sorting nexins, cluster IV components can be regarded as regulating late-Golgi trafficking events and interacting with the endosomal system.
evidence: This is inferred from the STRING network analysis.

claim: The category 'cell organization' extends the importance of vesicular transport as it contains factors involved in the architecture, organization, and homeostasis of the ER and Golgi apparatus, and the cytoskeleton-supporting these organelles.
source: Many of the cellular processes and host proteins assigned to 'transport' (specifically in clusters II-IV) are also listed in the category 'cell organization' (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a). However, this category actually extends the importance of vesicular transport as it also contains factors involved in the architecture, organization, and homeostasis of the ER and Golgi apparatus, and the cytoskeleton-supporting these organelles.
evidence: This is from the GO enrichment and STRING network analysis.

claim: A number of MHV RTC-proximal factors were part of the host translation machinery.
source: Notably, a number of MHV RTC-proximal factors were part of the host translation machinery and assigned to category 'translation' (Figure 3a, Figure 3c).
evidence: This is from the GO enrichment and STRING network analysis.

claim: There was enrichment of factors involved in translation initiation, particularly multiple subunits of eIF3 and eIF4 complexes, as well as eIF2, eIF5, the Ddx3y helicase, and the Elongation factor-like GTPase 1.
source: We found enrichment of factors involved in translation initiation, particularly multiple subunits of eIF3 and eIF4 complexes, as well as eIF2, eIF5, the Ddx3y helicase, and the Elongation factor-like GTPase 1, which are required for the formation of 43S pre-initiation complexes, 48S initiation complexes, and the assembly of elongation-competent 80S ribosomes (Jackson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is from the mass spectrometry data and supported by the cited reference.

claim: The enriched translation initiation factors are required for the formation of 43S pre-initiation complexes, 48S initiation complexes, and the assembly of elongation-competent 80S ribosomes.
source: We found enrichment of factors involved in translation initiation, particularly multiple subunits of eIF3 and eIF4 complexes, as well as eIF2, eIF5, the Ddx3y helicase, and the Elongation factor-like GTPase 1, which are required for the formation of 43S pre-initiation complexes, 48S initiation complexes, and the assembly of elongation-competent 80S ribosomes (Jackson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference describing the function of these factors.

claim: The high degree of interaction between translation initiation subunits is suggestive of the presence of the entire translation initiation apparatus in close proximity to the viral RTC.
source: The high degree of interaction between these subunits is suggestive of the presence of the entire translation initiation apparatus in close proximity to the viral RTC.
evidence: This is inferred from the STRING network analysis showing interactions between translation factors.

claim: The category 'catabolic processes' includes a subset of autophagy-related factors and numerous ubiquitin-dependent ERAD components.
source: Lastly, the category 'catabolic processes' (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b) includes a subset of autophagy-related factors and numerous ubiquitin-dependent ERAD components, including the E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase complex and 26S proteasome regulatory subunits (Psmc2, Psmd4).
evidence: This is from the GO enrichment and STRING network analysis.

claim: siRNA-mediated silencing of 53 RTC-proximal host factors significantly reduced MHV replication compared to non-targeting siRNA controls.
source: We found that siRNA-mediated silencing of 53 RTC-proximal host factors significantly reduced MHV replication compared to non-targeting siRNA controls.
evidence: This is from the siRNA screen data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The 53 host factors whose silencing reduced MHV replication can be considered proviral and required for efficient replication.
source: These factors can therefore be considered proviral and required for efficient replication (Figure 4b; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the siRNA screen results.

claim: No antiviral factors that resulted in significant enhancement of viral replication upon siRNA knockdown were found.
source: In contrast, we did not find antiviral factors that resulted in significant enhancement of viral replication upon siRNA knockdown.
evidence: This is from the siRNA screen results.

claim: siRNA targets that had the strongest impact on MHV replication were in majority contained within the functional categories highlighted in Figure 3a.
source: Notably, siRNA targets that had the strongest impact on MHV replication were in majority contained within the functional categories highlighted in Figure 3a (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is shown in the bubble plot in Figure 4b.

claim: Several factors in anterograde and retrograde vesicular transport pathways between the ER, Golgi apparatus and endosomal compartments impaired MHV replication when silenced.
source: Indeed, in line with the hypothesis that MHV subverts key components mediating both anterograde and retrograde vesicular transport between the ER, Golgi apparatus and endosomal compartments for the establishment of replication organelles, several factors contained within these pathways impaired MHV replication as exemplified by the siRNA-mediated silencing of Kif11, Snx9, Dnm11, Scfd1, Ykt6, Stx5a, Clint1, Aak11, or Vapa (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is from the siRNA screen data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: ER-associated protein sorting complexes associated with the ribosome and newly synthetized proteins (Naca, BTF3, SRP54a, SRP68) appear to be required for efficient MHV replication.
source: Consistently, ER-associated protein sorting complexes associated with the ribosome and newly synthetized proteins (Naca, BTF3, SRP54a, SRP68) that were revealed in the GO enrichment analysis (Figure 3a, Supplementary file 2), also appear to be required for efficient MHV replication (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is from the siRNA screen data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Silencing of core elements of the 26S and 20S proteasome complex (Psmd1 and Psmc2, and Psmb3, respectively) resulted in significantly reduced MHV replication.
source: Furthermore, we also observed significantly reduced MHV replication upon silencing of core elements of the 26S and 20S proteasome complex (Psmd1 and Psmc2, and Psmb3, respectively), suggesting a crucial role of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway for efficient CoV replication (Wong et al., 2015; Raaben et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is from the siRNA screen data and supported by cited references.

claim: The ubiquitin-proteasome pathway plays a crucial role for efficient coronavirus replication.
source: Furthermore, we also observed significantly reduced MHV replication upon silencing of core elements of the 26S and 20S proteasome complex (Psmd1 and Psmc2, and Psmb3, respectively), suggesting a crucial role of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway for efficient CoV replication (Wong et al., 2015; Raaben et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is inferred from the siRNA screen data and supported by cited references.

claim: Silencing of ribosomal proteins Rpl13a and Rls24d1 and several subunits of the eIF3 complex resulted in greatly reduced MHV replication.
source: Silencing of ribosomal proteins Rpl13a and Rls24d1 and several subunits of the eIF3 complex resulted in greatly reduced MHV replication and scored with highest significance in the siRNA screen
evidence: This is from the siRNA screen data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Proximity of the host cell translation machinery to the viral RTC likely has functional importance for coronavirus replication.
source: suggesting that proximity of the host cell translation machinery to the viral RTC likely has functional importance for coronavirus replication (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is inferred from the siRNA screen results showing that translation factors are required for replication.

claim: For Rpl13a, and eIFs 3i, 3f, and 3e, viral replication was reduced to levels comparable to controls Ceacam1a (MHV receptor) and Gbf1.
source: Specifically for Rpl13a, and eIFs 3i, 3 f, and 3e viral replication was reduced to levels comparable to our controls Ceacam1a (MHV receptor) and Gbf1 (Verheije et al., 2008).
evidence: This is from the validation experiments shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Cell-associated viral mRNA levels were reduced upon siRNA silencing of Rpl13a, eIF3i, eIF3f, and eIF3e.
source: Consistently, cell-associated viral mRNA levels (Figure 4d) and viral titers (Figure 4e) were reduced upon siRNA silencing of these factors.
evidence: This is shown in the validation experiments in Figure 4d.

claim: Viral titers were reduced upon siRNA silencing of Rpl13a, eIF3i, eIF3f, and eIF3e.
source: Consistently, cell-associated viral mRNA levels (Figure 4d) and viral titers (Figure 4e) were reduced upon siRNA silencing of these factors.
evidence: This is shown in the validation experiments in Figure 4e.

claim: Effective knockdown of translation factors did not affect cell viability.
source: Although the silencing of a subset of host translation factors severely restricted MHV replication, effective knockdown of these factors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c) did not affect cell viability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d)
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary data.

claim: Effective knockdown of translation factors only moderately affected host cell translation levels.
source: and only moderately affected host cell translation levels (Figure 4f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is shown in the puromycin incorporation assay in Figure 4f.

claim: The reduced viral replication observed after siRNA knockdown of translation factors is not due to a general impairment of host translation.
source: This data demonstrates that the reduced viral replication observed after siRNA knockdown is not due to a general impairment of host translation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing minimal effects on host translation despite reduced viral replication.

claim: Under conditions of eIF3e, eIF3f, and eIF3i knockdown, viral replication was significantly restricted.
source: Importantly, under conditions of eIF3e, eIF3f, and eIF3i knockdown, viral replication was also significantly restricted, confirming the importance of these translation initiation factors for MHV replication (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is shown in the validation experiments in Figure 5c.

claim: MHV-infected L929 cells displayed a pronounced enrichment of actively translating ribosomes near the viral RTC.
source: In striking contrast, MHV-infected L929 cells displayed a pronounced enrichment of actively translating ribosomes near the viral RTC as indicated by the strong overlap between the viral replicase and the ribopuromycylation stain.
evidence: This is shown by the ribopuromycylation assay in Figure 6.

claim: Active translation in vicinity of the RTC was strongest during the early phase of infection at 6 h.p.i., and was observed until 8 h.p.i.
source: Interestingly, active translation in vicinity of the RTC was strongest during the early phase of infection at 6 h.p.i., and was observed until 8 h.p.i., before gradually decreasing as the infection advanced along with the appearance of typical syncytia formation indicative of cytopathic effect (CPE).
evidence: This is shown in the time course ribopuromycylation data in Figure 6.

claim: A similar phenotype of active translation near the RTC was observed in Huh7 cells infected with HCoV-229E or MERS-CoV.
source: Remarkably, we observed a similar phenotype in Huh7 cells infected with human coronaviruses, such as HCoV-229E or the highly pathogenic MERS-CoV (Figure 7).
evidence: This is shown by the ribopuromycylation assay in Figure 7.

claim: A striking co-localization of the HCoV-229E RTC with sites of active translation was observed during the early phase of the infection.
source: Consistent with findings obtained for MHV, we observed a striking co-localization of the HCoV-229E RTC with sites of active translation during the early phase of the infection (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by the ribopuromycylation assay in Figure 7.

claim: Active translation is localized to the site of MERS-CoV RNA synthesis as dsRNA puncta highly overlapped with the ribopuromycylation stain in MERS-CoV-infected Huh7 cells.
source: Finally, we further demonstrated that active translation is localized to the site of MERS-CoV RNA synthesis as dsRNA puncta highly overlapped with the ribopuromycylation stain in MERS-CoV-infected Huh7 cells (Figure 7).
evidence: This is shown by the ribopuromycylation assay in Figure 7.

claim: The results confirm the spatial link between individual components of the host cell translation machinery and coronavirus replication compartments.
source: Collectively, these results not only confirm the spatial link between individual components of the host cell translation machinery and coronavirus replication compartments as identified by proximity-dependent biotinylation using MHV-BirAR118G-nsp2
evidence: This is inferred from the combined proximity labeling and ribopuromycylation data.

claim: Active translation is taking place in close proximity to the viral RTC.
source: but they also demonstrate that active translation is taking place in close proximity to the viral RTC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ribopuromycylation assays in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The list of RTC-proximal proteins by far exceeds the number of host cell proteins currently known to interact with viral replication complexes.
source: Importantly, our list of RTC-proximal proteins by far exceeds the number of host cell proteins currently known to interact with viral replication complexes and the vast majority of MHV RTC-proximal proteins have not been described before.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the 513 identified proteins to previously published studies.

claim: The vast majority of MHV RTC-proximal proteins have not been described before.
source: Importantly, our list of RTC-proximal proteins by far exceeds the number of host cell proteins currently known to interact with viral replication complexes and the vast majority of MHV RTC-proximal proteins have not been described before.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the identified proteins to previously published studies.

claim: Coronaviruses may have evolved a two-pronged strategy to ensure efficient translation of viral proteins by establishing viral RNA synthesis in close proximity to actively translating ribosomes and by employing nsp1-mediated host cell mRNA degradation at RTC-distal sites.
source: Coronaviruses may thus have evolved a two-pronged strategy to ensure efficient translation of viral proteins by establishing viral RNA synthesis in close proximity to actively translating ribosomes and by employing nsp1-mediated host cell mRNA degradation at RTC-distal sites.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the data showing active translation near the RTC and known nsp1 function.

claim: The strategy to assemble the viral RTC in close proximity to translation would favor the coupling between genome translation and replication that has been proposed for picornaviruses and other positive-strand RNA viruses.
source: The strategy to assemble the viral RTC in close proximity to translation would also favor the coupling between genome translation and replication that has been proposed for picornaviruses and other positive-strand RNA viruses (de Groot et al., 1992; Novak and Kirkegaard, 1994).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by cited references to similar mechanisms in other viruses.

claim: Proximity of viral mRNA synthesis and translation in a confined microenvironment protected from cytosolic surveillance factors can be considered a mechanism to evade cytosolic mRNA decay mechanisms and innate immune sensors of viral RNA.
source: Therefore, proximity of viral mRNA synthesis and translation in a confined microenvironment protected from cytosolic surveillance factors can also be considered a mechanism to evade these cytosolic mRNA decay mechanisms and innate immune sensors of viral RNA.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the data and knowledge of innate immune sensing.
